lessons: Prioritize immediate, contrast-based hooks: The top-performing video ('This Shark Can Live For Centuries!') and 'Why Tuna Meat Is Red Meat' show the highest early retention when the hook establishes an immediate, high-stakes curiosity gap or surprising visual category comparison.

Eliminate slow exposition: Drop-off data shows that lines explaining technical mechanisms (e.g., 'To turn that watery sap into thick syrup...') consistently trigger viewer exits. Keep technical explanations secondary to the immediate hook.

Avoid redundant explanations: The data shows significant abandonment when scripts re-explain concepts that were already implied or stated in the hook, such as in the 'Why your eyes are secretly leaking' and 'Why Onions Make You Cry' videos.

Maintain high stakes through the end: Videos like the shark study keep viewers until the end because they sustain a high-level mystery, whereas videos that pivot to slow, mechanical details (e.g., 'Why Fingers Prune In Water') see a total collapse of retention at the 50% mark.

Anchor scientific claims to physical action: Lines that focus on the 'why' of a physical sensation (e.g., pineapple 'eating you back') hold viewers better than lines focused on abstract definitions or chemical compositions.
worst_moment_types: Technical process breakdowns (e.g., boiling sap, cell storage of chemicals)
Secondary explanation of the hook premise
Lines correcting common misconceptions that require multiple sentences to explain
Abstract definitions that lack immediate sensory context
best_hook_types: Direct category contradictions (e.g., 'Tuna vs Cod', 'Garlic vs Onions')
Extreme superlative claims (e.g., 'This shark is older than the United States')
Provocative personification of inanimate objects (e.g., 'Fresh pineapple is eating you back')
